channel.title: InvestPR Media Monitoring
channel.description: Capital kept landing this period: Islandwide put $1.7M (plus $580K in Act 60 incentives) into automated logistics sorting in Ponce and Arecibo, adding 80 jobs; PRISA Group broke ground on the $20M Distrito Sports Hub with Banco Popular financing; Fazoli's opened its first island location on a $5.4M investment backed by the BDE and SBA 504; and Autocare added a $6M facility in Caguas. On the macro side, Fitch restored First BanCorp to investment grade, citing a more diversified economy, and new DDEC Secretary Ríos Pierluisi is telling investors existing decrees hold, with 20-plus companies in the pipeline and Roosevelt Roads work slated to resume early next year.

item.title: Desarrollo Económico e Islandwide inauguran innovador sistema de empaque que agilizará y aumentará el manejo de carga en Puerto Rico
item.description:
Governor Jenniffer González, DDEC Secretary Carlos J. Ríos Pierluisi, and Islandwide CEO Pedro Rosaly inaugurated an automated conveyor package-sorting system at the Puerto Rican logistics firm, a $1.65 million investment in machinery supported by $580,000 in Law 60 incentives from the DDEC that will create 80 jobs and retain 397 existing ones. Operating from PRIDCO facilities in Ponce and Arecibo, Islandwide projects tripling its processing capacity to serve critical industries such as medical devices, pharma, and advanced manufacturing. The announcement showcases government-backed logistics modernization that strengthens Puerto Rico's positioning as the Caribbean's leading logistics and supply-chain hub — key infrastructure evidence for companies evaluating the island.

item.title: Islandwide invests $1.7M in logistics automation project
item.description:
Puerto Rican logistics firm Islandwide launched an automated package-sorting system backed by $1.65 million of its own capital and $580,000 in DDEC incentives, creating 80 jobs, retaining 397 positions, and tripling its processing capacity. DDEC Secretary Carlos J. Ríos-Pierluisi and Gov. Jenniffer González-Colón framed the project as advancing Puerto Rico's positioning as a regional logistics and supply-chain hub. It matters for investment attraction because it demonstrates working government incentives and modernizing logistics infrastructure that support e-commerce, pharma, and advanced-manufacturing supply chains on the island.

item.description:

item.title: Corruption allegations put investment in Puerto Rico under scrutiny
item.description:
Financial specialists including Birling Capital's Francisco Rodríguez, former PRIDCO director Eric Santiago, and attorney Rafael Ferreira Cintrón warn that corruption allegations and forged signatures in decrees at the DDEC are eroding investor trust, with Santiago's business survey finding 83% perceive diminished confidence in the incentive program. The Puerto Rico Manufacturers Association urged rigorous, transparent investigation while stressing that the Law 60 legal framework remains sound for companies already operating on the Island. This directly threatens Puerto Rico's investment attraction: institutional investors respond to such scandals by pausing deployments, demanding higher risk premiums, and carrying lasting negative memory of the jurisdiction in future site-selection decisions.

item.title: Eventualmente...
item.description:

item.title: Proyecto de incentivos al reciclaje en Puerto Rico genera preocupación en Basura Cero
item.description:

It matters for investment attraction because the bill's fate will shape the incentive landscape and regulatory clarity for circular-economy and recycling ventures considering Puerto Rico.

item.title: Puerto Rico recycling incentives bill draws concerns from waste advocate
item.description:
House Bill 1323 would create a recycling-industry incentives act offering tax credits, exemptions and a DDEC-attached special fund seeded with $20 million to encourage companies to use recycled materials as industrial feedstock in Puerto Rico. Basura Cero Puerto Rico's chair, Brenda Reyes-Tomassini, raised concerns that the bill could permit importing up to 30% of waste, misconstrues competitive EPA SWIFR grants as a funding source, and was drafted without coordination with the DNER's solid waste management plan. The debate matters for investment attraction because the incentive package targets a new circular-economy sector, but unresolved funding and permitting questions could create uncertainty for recycling companies considering Puerto Rico.

item.title: Inversión privada de USD 2,100 millones financiará obra eléctrica entre República Dominicana y Puerto Rico
item.description:
Caribbean Transmission formally presented Proyecto Hostos, a privately financed $2.1 billion undersea HVDC interconnection between the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico, featuring a 200 km, 700 MW cable fed by new dedicated generation in the DR, with operation targeted around 2027 and prior approval from the Trump administration. Backers say it would supply roughly 20% of Puerto Rico's electricity demand, displace diesel and bunker-C plants, cut up to 3.8 million tons of CO2 annually, and provide mutual backup between the two grids during emergencies. It matters for investment attraction because unreliable, expensive power is the top concern companies weigh when considering Puerto Rico, and a major private-capital project addressing grid capacity and resilience directly improves that calculus.

item.title: Washington Promised Puerto Rico $14 Billion To Fix Its Grid. Most of the Money Is Still Stuck.
item.description:
A new GAO audit found that about 75 percent of the $14 billion in federal funds obligated since 2017 to repair and modernize Puerto Rico's power grid — $10.7 billion — remains undisbursed, with FEMA the slowest agency and only nine of its funded projects completed as of December 2025. The article blames layered federal reviews, a 2024 Puerto Rico construction excise tax on recovery projects, legal battles with Luma Energy, and Jones Act shipping costs, noting islanders average 27 hours of outages per year versus two on the mainland while paying up to 31 percent more for electricity. Reliable, affordable power is a top site-selection criterion, so this high-profile account of grid dysfunction and slow recovery directly undermines Puerto Rico's investment attraction case.
